Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Leo hadn’t meant to become a patient. Two years prior, at eighteen, a sudden fever had dropped him into an intensive care unit, where the air grew sharp with antiseptic and the mechanical hum of monitors replaced his own breathing. He remembered the weight of the IV line threading into his forearm, the cold plastic of the drip bag swaying beside him, and the way the medical team moved quickly around his bed during rounds. The illness peaked with a night of racing chest pains and gasping for air, leaving him certain he would not wake up. When he was finally discharged, the relief was immediate but fragile. Within weeks, the fragility surfaced. Leo found himself jolting awake at the first knock at the door, his heart hammering as if the monitors were still counting down. He tried to push through, taking a part-time counseling position at a community youth center, hoping to fill the days with routine. But the clinic’s waiting room held a faint, lingering scent of disinfectant that once made him gag. He began avoiding the front desk, claiming the elevator was out of order instead. When students needed to submit medical notes for the center’s health waiver, Leo’s hands would go cold, his breath catching at the sight of the laminated clipboards. Needles and medical drips became impossible to watch, even on screen. When his girlfriend, Clara, suggested he schedule a routine physical examination, the mere thought of undergoing the procedure tightened his chest. His body, once a steady companion, now felt like a traitor. He was certain it would fail him again, that a simple cold could spiral into that same suffocating fear. To keep the terror at bay, Leo built routines around absence. He delayed sleep, staying up until very late, scrolling through his phone just to outrun the quiet hours when his mind finally slowed. The startle response grew sharper; a colleague stepping too quickly to his shoulder made him flinch violently, knocking over a stack of referral forms on his desk. He stopped attending his own weekly sessions with the center’s on-site therapist, finding himself mentally shutting down the moment the conversation neared his hospital stay. He told himself he was just protecting his progress, though the silence left him more hollow. His work, which once grounded him in helping others navigate uncertainty, now felt entirely meaningless. The stories of struggling students echoed but left no echo in him. He watched them worry about exams and friendships, certain he had lost the capacity to care about anything that did not involve survival. His body kept reacting as if he were still in the hospital bed, even when he was safely behind his desk. The administrative wing required him to walk past the staff health clinic to reach his office. He had come to believe that safety was a temporary illusion, and that his nervous system was locked in a loop of false alarms. He no longer trusted his own body to distinguish between a quiet afternoon and a medical crisis. The avoidance strategies sat alongside his exhaustion, leaving him isolated in his own skin. Clara noticed the distance, the way he flinched when she reached for him in bed, and how he refused to take the car past the emergency room on the way to their apartment. He finally sat across from his new therapist, not because the fear had lessened, but because the exhaustion had finally outweighed it. He wanted to stop bracing for a collapse that never came. He wanted to trust his chest again, to feel the weight of a needle or the smell of a clinic without his pulse spiking. What he hoped for most was simply to exist in his own life without feeling like a patient in it.
